content.thinking:
This looks like a disproven alarm — no user actually experienced a failure, yet the error-rate alert fired anyway. I'm tracing the causal chain starting from T6 and AL1: the rule triggered without the underlying service actually erroring, so I need to figure out why the alert fired when nothing was wrong on the user side.

Evidence doesn't show why the rule fired - not even the rule's own metric series showed any departure from baseline, so the trail stops there. Chain length is only 1-2 steps, and it doesn't reach a definitive cause. I'm now weighing whether the lack of paging counts as a contributing factor, but since nobody was actually harmed in this false alarm, it doesn't seem to qualify - the root cause seems to just be that the rule fired on something invisible in its own data.

Action items should focus on investigating why the rule fired and checking paging routing, while noting I shouldn't flag unread deploys/flags/logs as something that "went wrong" since I never examined them. For went-well, Argus did successfully disprove the alarm by reading metrics after the alert fired. For went-wrong, the key finding is that no on-call incident was linked despite the rule firing. For still-at-risk, I can note that since the firing cause remains unknown, the rule could fire falsely again.

action_items.item: Find out why the HighErrorRate rule on io-shop fired when its own series in the window Argus read showed no breach, by comparing what the rule evaluated at the time it fired with the series as stored.
Find out why no on-call page was linked to the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop, and route the alert to on-call if it is meant to page.

causal_chain.step: Nobody using io-shop was seen to hit a failure. What happened instead was that the HighErrorRate alert fired, claiming the error rate had been above threshold for {A1}. In the window Argus read, no minute departed from the service's baseline in errors, p50, p95, p99 or memory.

The alert fired without a failure behind it. The alert rule's own series, read over the same window, did not show the breach the alarm claimed. The evidence stops here: the record does not show why the rule fired.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An alarm about errors went off even though the service's measurements, including the ones the alarm itself watches, showed nothing out of the ordinary, and the record does not show why it went off.

went_well: Argus read the service's per-minute metrics and found, {T6.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, that nothing in the window matched the alarm's claim. That let it close the incident as disproven without taking any action on production.
went_wrong: The HighErrorRate alert fired but nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to it. Had the failure been real, nobody on call would have been brought in by a page.

input.root_cause: The evidence does not show why the HighErrorRate rule fired: across the window Argus read, no minute departed from the service's baseline in errors, p50, p95, p99, memory or the alert rule's own series, so no mechanism of failure was found and the alarm was disproven.
input.still_at_risk: Nobody found out why the rule fired, so it could fire again when nothing has failed.
input.symptom: Nobody using io-shop saw a failure; an error-rate alarm fired with no errors rising
